ARTCLINE secures additional €3.4 million in funds to support commercialization of its ARTICE® immune cell therapy for treatment of septic shock
ARTCLINE GmbH secures €3.4 million in new financing from existing and new investors, including a €1 million investment from MBG MV
Funding will support market launch of ARTCLINE’s ARTICE® therapy, which will build on the successful finalization of the ReActIF-ICE clinical trial
Rostock (Germany), September 9, 2026 –

ARTCLINE, a biomedical company focused on the development of novel immune cell therapies for the treatment of septic shock, announces the successful completion of a new financing round totaling €3.4 million. The financing round includes a €1 million investment from Mittelständische Beteiligungsgesellschaft Mecklenburg-Vorpommern mbH (MBG MV) and further commitments from both existing and new investors.

The funds will be used to support the launch of ARTICE®, the company’s immune cell-based therapy for the treatment of septic shock. ARTCLINE is preparing to publish the topline results from its multicenter, randomized, controlled validation study ReActIF-ICE (
) involving 142 patients, which has been recently completed and is currently in read out.
We would like to thank
MBG MV and all investors for their continued trust and commitment to ARTCLINE in our joint mission to address septic shock, one of the most critical challenges in intensive care medicine,
” said Jens Altrichter, MD, Managing Director and Founder of ARTCLINE GmbH. “
Over the years, we have seen growing evidence for the efficacy of ARTICE

and are very confident that our ReActIF-ICE study will confirm earlier clinical results. Upon publication of the study results, which are expected later this year, I am very much looking forward to discussing the results with the medical community.”
Dirk Hessel, Managing Director of ARTCLINE GmbH, added: “
The successful completion of this financing round provides us with the resources required
to advance
preparation

s for commercialization, with the intended launch in early 2027, and to strengthen our organization's growth trajectory. We are excited about the opportunity to make this new treatment option available for the treatment of patients suffering from septic shock.”

Sepsis and septic shock remain major challenges in intensive care medicine, with a significant unmet medical need. ARTCLINE is developing ARTICE®, an allogeneic immune cell therapy designed to support key functions of the dysregulated immune system in patients with septic shock.
About ARTCLINE GmbH

ARTCLINE GmbH develops novel immune cell therapies for use in critical care medicine. The company focuses on the treatment of septic shock – one of the major challenges for global health systems. With the ARTICE® therapy, ARTCLINE uses allogeneic immune cells from healthy donors to specifically support and stabilize key functions of patients’ dysregulated immune systems. The therapeutic approach was developed in close collaboration with immunologists and clinical specialists.

All essential components of the ARTICE® therapy have received the necessary regulatory approvals. The donor immune cells are manufactured under the applicable GMP manufacturing authorization, while the relevant medical device components used in the ARTICE® procedure are CE marked.

About Sepsis and Septic Shock

Despite continuous advances in research and medicine, the mortality rate associated with sepsis remains high. According to the WHO, approximately 48 million people suffer from sepsis each year, including about 20 million children under the age of five. It is estimated that one in five deaths worldwide is associated with sepsis.[1] In Germany alone, between 70,000 and 220,000 people die from sepsis each year.[2] Dysregulation of the immune system plays a central role in the course of the disease, particularly in the most severe form of sepsis, septic shock. While many patients survive the initial phase of septic shock thanks to modern intensive care measures, serious complications such as secondary infections and recurrent organ failure frequently occur later on, contributing significantly to the high mortality rate.
